evidence: src/infrastructure/http/app.ts: createApp(controllers) chains express.json, createRouter(controllers), notFoundHandler and errorHandler. It only builds the app and adds no routes of its own.
src/infrastructure/http/routes.ts: createRouter({ users, projects, tasks }: Controllers) is the only place where route-to-handler mappings are defined.

src/infrastructure/http/requestParsing.ts: requireString and optionalString share one asFields helper and throw RequestValidationError. All three controllers import these helpers, so the field checks live in one place.
src/infrastructure/http/RequestValidationError.ts: the one error class for malformed requests, used by both requestParsing.ts and middleware/errorHandler.ts.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: All four files deal with one concern: the HTTP delivery adapter in the infrastructure layer. app.ts builds the Express app and wires up middleware. routes.ts maps URLs to controller handlers through the Controllers interface. requestParsing.ts holds the shared helpers that check the shape of request fields. RequestValidationError.ts defines the single error type for malformed requests. Each rule lives in one place: field checks are only in requestParsing.ts, which every controller imports, and the malformed-request error is only in RequestValidationError.ts, which both the parser and errorHandler use. Route registration is only in routes.ts, and app assembly is only in app.ts. Nothing goes around the module's own pieces: app.ts uses createRouter instead of registering routes itself, and parsing always throws the module's own error type. No business logic has leaked into these files.
